title: Meet the Siddis: Tribal Gujaratis from Kathiawad, natural athletes of African stock
syllabus: GS1 › Salient features of Indian society; diversity · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections (Scheduled Tribes, PVTGs) · GS4 › Inclusive governance; equity; compassion towards the weaker sections
summary: Khushbu Darjada, 15, became the first Siddi athlete to win a Youth Olympics medal (judo silver); the Siddis of Gujarat, of African descent, are a PVTG of about 12,959 people.
ideas: Diversity of Indian society: the Siddis, of East African descent, speak Gujarati with a Kathiawadi accent and share local food and dress; their faith blends Sufi Islam with local Hindu elements.
GS1 · Diversity / syncretism
The Siddis of Kathiawad show India's diversity: African roots, Gujarati culture and a Sufi-Hindu blend.
History of arrival: views differ, Portuguese colonists as slaves, overland via invaders, or as bodyguards invited by the nawabs of Junagadh; there is no definitive record.
GS1 · History / migration
The Siddis' many origin stories show how slavery, trade and princely courts shaped Indian society.

Classification and inclusion: declared ST in 1956 and a 'primitive tribal group' in 1982; Siddis in Saurashtra are STs but those outside are SEBC, so the same community gets different protection by place.
GS2 · Scheduled Tribes / PVTGs
Siddis are STs in Saurashtra but SEBC elsewhere in Gujarat: classification by geography can fragment protection.
Sport as a ladder: young Siddis are selected for sports camps, but many drop out, unable to cope with the discipline; the Darjada sisters show what sustained support can achieve.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections / GS4 · Inclusive governance
Sports camps open a door for Siddi youth; mentoring and support must keep it open.
Education as change: Afsana Makwa became the first Siddi woman to clear the Gujarat PSC exam; more youths are completing higher education, though such families are still few.
GS1 · Social change / GS4 · Equity
The first Siddi woman to clear the state PSC shows education turning a marginalised community into a participating one.
keywords: PVTG
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, marked by small, stagnant population and low development
GS2 · Tribal welfare
The Siddis are among 75 PVTGs who need targeted, culturally sensitive development.
Equity vs equality
Equity gives extra support to those who start behind; equality treats all alike
GS4 · Inclusive governance
Sports quotas and coaching for Siddi youth are equity, not favour.
Syncretism
Blending of different religious and cultural traditions
GS1 · Indian society
Siddi rituals that mix Sufi Islam and Hindu practice are an example of Indian syncretism.
examples: Khushbu Darjada, Youth Olympics 2026
First Siddi athlete, and only the second Indian, to win a Youth Olympics judo medal
GS4
GS2 · Vulnerable sections · GS4 · Inclusive governance
Khushbu Darjada's medal shows that inclusive governance, giving opportunity to the margins, enriches the nation.
Afsana Makwa
First woman from the Siddi community to clear the Gujarat Public Service Commission exam
GS4
GS1 · Women and social change · GS4 · Equity
Afsana Makwa's success shows education as the surest ladder for marginalised women.
pyqs: Does tribal development policy reflect equity-based governance?
When diverse tribes can be treated as one category.
Legal initiatives against discrimination of STs.

trend.t: Tribal questions moved from constitutional basis (2016) and discrimination (2017) to whether diverse tribes can be one category (2022), displacement (2025) and, in 2026, whether tribal policy reflects equity-based governance.
trend.watch: The 2026 question asked about equity in tribal policy, so examples of inclusion, and of gaps like differing ST status by region, are valuable.
focus: Sport and education as ladders of mobility

potential: "Inclusive governance is measured by the opportunities it creates at the margins." Discuss with reference to Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. (10 marks)

title: Gender struggles must forge solidarities, not exclusion
where: Ideas page, page 9 (Swarupa Deb, human rights lawyer and sociologist)
syllabus: GS2 › Fundamental rights; mechanisms for protection of vulnerable sections (transgender persons) · GS1 › Social empowerment; women · GS4 › Social justice; equity; inclusive governance
summary: A women's group has asked the Supreme Court to stop recognising trans women as 'females' in official documents; the author argues debate must treat transgender persons as equal rights-bearers, not as a threat to women.
ideas: The petition: a women's group argues that recognising trans women as females could affect sex-based reservation, sporting categories, women-only spaces and safeguards for women.
GS2 · Rights in conflict
The petition sets women's sex-based protections against trans women's legal recognition.
Feminism's own critique: feminist movements contested the idea that biology or reproductive capacity determines women's social position, which in turn helped the transgender movement.
GS1 · Women's movements
Feminism argued anatomy is not destiny, a principle that also underpins transgender recognition.

History of solidarity: trans and cis feminists worked together on bodily autonomy in the 1970s; in November 2019 Indian women's groups opposed making recognition depend on certification by authorities and medical documents.
GS1 · Social movements / GS2 · Self-identification
In 2019, Indian women's groups stood with trans persons for self-determined gender identity.
Equality is indivisible: the constitutional guarantee of equality cannot be upheld if one marginalised group's protection is secured at the expense of another.
GS2 · Equality (Art 14) / GS4 · Social justice
Rights secured by excluding another marginalised group weaken equality for all.

Debate, but on equal terms: the issues of gender identity, sex-based classification and legal protections need reasoned debate premised on recognising transgender persons as equal rights-bearing subjects.
GS2 · Rights / GS4 · Inclusive governance
Hard questions on gender and law deserve debate, but only one that begins from equal dignity.
keywords: Self-identification of gender
The right to determine one's own gender identity without medical certification
GS2 · Rights of transgender persons
Self-identification of gender was upheld as part of dignity and autonomy.
Intersectional solidarity
Joint action by groups facing overlapping discrimination
GS1 · Social movements
Intersectional solidarity between women's and trans rights movements strengthens both.
Bodily autonomy
The right to make decisions about one's own body
GS2 · Article 21
Bodily autonomy links reproductive rights and gender identity under Article 21.
examples: Women's groups' statement, November 2019
Opposed provisions making transgender recognition depend on state and medical certification
GS4
GS1 · Social movements · GS4 · Solidarity and empathy
The 2019 statement by women's groups shows empathy across struggles, a value inclusive governance needs.
pyqs: Effect of 2026 amendment to Transgender Persons Act 2019 on self-identity and privacy (Art 21).
Constitutional perspectives on gender justice, provisions and case laws.
Are welfare schemes for vulnerable sections discriminatory by nature?
Gender equality, gender equity and women's empowerment.

trend.t: Gender questions broadened from women's empowerment (2019, 2024) to constitutional gender justice (2023) and, in 2026, the rights of transgender persons under the amended Transgender Persons Act.
trend.watch: Transgender rights were asked directly in 2026, and rights-in-conflict framing is UPSC's favoured pattern, so the recognition debate is high-yield.
focus: Transgender Persons Act and its 2026 amendment

potential: "The constitutional guarantee of equality cannot be upheld by securing one marginalised group's rights at the expense of another." Discuss in the context of transgender rights. (15 marks)

title: How welfare board will function, what changes for unorganised, gig workers
where: Economy, page 10 (Ravi Dutta Mishra & Aanchal Magazine)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies
summary: Follow-up: the Labour Ministry has notified two social security boards (40 members for unorganised workers, 22 for gig and platform workers) under the Code on Social Security.
evolution: Labour Ministry notifies the National Social Security Board under the Code on Social Security (Economy, page 23).
Details: two boards, aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and EPFO coverage widened.
ideas: Two boards, not one: a 40-member board for unorganised workers and a 22-member board for gig and platform workers, which includes aggregators such as quick-commerce and delivery platforms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Separate boards recognise that gig and platform workers need schemes designed for platform work.
Who pays: aggregators must contribute 1–2% of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5% of what they pay workers; the fund also draws on governments, CSR and fines.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregator contributions put part of the cost of gig workers' security on the platforms that profit from them.
What it covers: schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and crèches.
GS2 · Welfare
Social security for gig workers spans life-cycle risks, from maternity to old age.
Wider formal coverage: EPFO provisions now apply to all establishments with 20 or more employees, regardless of industry, not only those in the old schedule.
GS3 · Labour reforms
Extending EPFO to all establishments with 20+ workers widens formal social security.
keywords: Social Security Fund
Pooled fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers
GS2 · Welfare
A dedicated Social Security Fund gives gig workers' schemes a stable financing base.
Aggregator levy
Platforms paying a share of turnover towards workers' welfare
GS3 · Labour
The aggregator levy shares the cost of social protection with platforms.
data: Aggregators' contribution to the social security fund, capped at 5% of amounts payable to workers
Code on Social Security, via IE
Aggregators must contribute 1–2% of turnover to gig workers' social security, capped at 5% of payouts (Code on Social Security).
examples: Aggregators on the gig workers' board
Platforms sit with worker bodies to design welfare schemes
GS2 · Tripartism, statutory bodies · GS3 · Digital economy
Putting aggregators and worker bodies on one board shows tripartism adapting to the platform economy.
pyqs: The gig economy and women's empowerment.

title: 'I didn't sit on my sofa for a year': The cost of living with OCD
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to health (mental health) · GS4 › Empathy; Attitude and stigma
summary: Minor topic: personal accounts show how shame, misdiagnosis and late treatment turn obsessive-compulsive disorder into years of distress.
ideas: More than neatness: OCD is a mental health condition where intrusive thoughts trigger anxiety and repetitive rituals that bring only brief relief.
GS2 · Mental health
Popular misuse of 'OCD' trivialises a disabling mental illness.
The treatment gap: shame, misdiagnosis and confusion with religious practice delay care; most people live with symptoms for long before their first session.
GS2 · Health access
Stigma and low awareness widen India's mental-health treatment gap.
Treatable with the right care: medication with exposure and response prevention therapy is the standard; psychoeducation for families matters; advanced options such as deep TMS are free at AIIMS.
GS2 · Health services
Combining medication, therapy and family education makes OCD manageable.
keywords: Treatment gap
Share of people with a condition who get no care
GS2 · Mental health
Delayed diagnosis widens the mental-health treatment gap.
Psychoeducation
Teaching patients and families about the condition
GS2 · Health / GS4
Psychoeducation reduces stigma and improves treatment success.
data: Prevalence of OCD among Indian adults
National Mental Health Survey (2015-16), via IE
The National Mental Health Survey estimated OCD prevalence among Indian adults at 0.8%.
examples: Stigma delaying care
Young people hiding symptoms for years before diagnosis
GS4
GS2 · Mental health · GS4 · Empathy, attitude and stigma
OCD accounts show that empathy and awareness, not just medicines, decide whether people seek help.
